questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the branches of the vagal nerve from the superior vagal ganglion.
questions.explanation: The vagal nerve (CN X) exits the skull via the jugular foramen. Its superior (jugular) ganglion gives off only meningeal and auricular branches before the nerve continues inferiorly as the cervical vagus.
questions.keyConcept: Vagal nerve ganglia and extracranial branches
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal nerve and Auricular nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What’s the arterial supply of thalamus?
questions.explanation: The thalamus receives arterial blood from perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), specifically the posteromedial (for medial/anterior thalamus) and posterolateral (thalamogeniculate) groups, which are branches of the P2 segment of the PCA.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamic blood supply via PCA branches
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial and anterior regions by posteromedial group of posterior cerebral artery
Lateral and posterior regions by posterolateral group of posterior cerebral artery (thalamogeniculate artery)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What’s the venous drainage of thalamus?
questions.explanation: Venous drainage of the thalamus is primarily via the thalamostriate vein (also called the terminal vein), which drains into the internal cerebral vein and subsequently contributes to the vein of Galen.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamic venous drainage via thalamostriate vein
questions.modelAnswer: Thalamostriate vein

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the boundaries of lateral ventricle.
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricle boundaries include: lateral wall (caudate nucleus), medial wall (septum pellucidum), roof (corpus callosum), floor (thalamus and hypothalamus), anterior wall (paraterminal gyrus), and posterior wall (splenium of corpus callosum).
questions.modelAnswer:
Lateral wall: thalamus and hypothalamus
Roof: Layer of ependyma. Choroid plexus hangs from its roof.
Floor: optic chiasma, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mamillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, tegmentum of midbrain
Anterior wall: lamina terminalis, column of fornix, anterior commissure
Posterior wall: posterior commissure, pineal body, suprapineal recess

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the recesses of third ventricle.
questions.explanation: The third ventricle has four recesses: optic recess (between optic chiasma and lamina terminalis), infundibular recess (into the pituitary stalk), pineal recess (into the pineal body), and suprapineal recess (above the pineal body).
questions.keyConcept: Third ventricle recesses and their locations
questions.modelAnswer:
Optic recess
Infundibular recess
Pineal recess
Suprapineal recess

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the connections of septal areas?
questions.explanation: The septal areas connect to the hypothalamus via the medial forebrain bundle and to the habenular nuclei via the stria medullaris thalami, forming key components of the limbic circuitry.
questions.keyConcept: Septal area connections and limbic circuitry
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial forebrain bundle: connects septal areas and amygdala with the hypothalamus
Stria medullaris thalami: connects septal areas to the habenular nuclei

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention 1 connection carried out by the fornix.
questions.explanation: The fornix carries the major output tract of the hippocampus, connecting it to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix, thus completing the Papez circuit involved in memory and emotion.
questions.modelAnswer: Hippocampus and mamillary bodies

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does lesion of hippocampus or papez circuit cause?
questions.explanation: Lesions to the hippocampus or Papez circuit cause anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) while preserving old memories, reflecting the hippocampus's critical role in memory consolidation.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterograde amnesia(loss of recent memory and preservation of old memory)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does the limbic lobe consist of?
questions.explanation: The limbic lobe consists of a C-shaped ring of cortical tissue including the subcallosal area, cingulate gyrus, isthmus, parahippocampal gyrus, and uncus, forming the emotional processing center of the brain.
questions.modelAnswer:
Subcallosal area (paraolfactory gyrus)
Cingulate gyrus
Isthmus
Parahippocampal gyrus
Uncus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Enumerate the long association fibers.
questions.explanation: The five major long association fibers are: superior longitudinal fasciculus (connecting frontal to parietal/occipital/temporal), inferior longitudinal fasciculus (temporal to occipital), fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus (frontal to temporal), and cingulum (cingulate to entorhinal cortex).
questions.keyConcept: Long association fibers and their connectivity
questions.modelAnswer: Superior longitudinal bundle, inferior longitudinal bundle, fronto occipital bundle, uncinate bundle, cingulum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the blood supply of internal capsule.
questions.explanation: The internal capsule blood supply varies by region: the upper anterior and posterior limbs receive MCA branches; the lower anterior limb and genu receive ACA branches; the lower posterior limb receives the anterior choroidal artery; and the retrolentiform/sublentiform parts receive the anterior choroidal artery.
questions.modelAnswer:
Upper half of anterior limb and upper half of posterior limb: MCA
Lower ½ of anterior limb and genu: ACA
Lower ½ of posterior limb: Post communicating and anterior choroidal artery
Retrolentiform and Sublentiform: Anterior choroidal artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the relations of corpus callosum
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is related superiorly to the falx cerebri and anterior cerebral arteries, and inferiorly to the fornix and septum pellucidum, making it a key anatomical landmark in the interhemispheric fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Corpus callosum superior and inferior relations
questions.modelAnswer:
Superiorly: Falx cerebri and Anterior cerebral arteries
Inferiorly: Fornix and septum pellucidum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the subarachnoid cisterns
questions.explanation: The major subarachnoid cisterns include the cerebellomedullary cistern (below cerebellum), cisterna magna (between cerebellum and medulla), pontine cistern, interpeduncular cistern, and cistern of the lateral fossa.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cerebello medullary cistern
Cistern of great cerebral vein
Cisterna pontis
Interpeduncular cistern
Cistern of lateral fossa

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: How is the CSF formed?
questions.explanation: CSF is actively secreted by the choroid plexus epithelial cells in the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles, primarily via Na+/K+ ATPase-driven transport mechanisms producing approximately 500 mL daily.
questions.modelAnswer: By choroid plexus of ventricles

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the circulation of CSF
questions.explanation: CSF flows from lateral ventricles through interventricular foramina to third ventricle, then via cerebral aqueduct to fourth ventricle, exiting through median/lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
questions.modelAnswer: Lateral ventricles > interventricular foramen>third ventricle > aqueduct of sylvius > fourth ventricle > Median foramen of magendie and two lateral foramen of lucshka > subarachnoid space

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the absorption of CSF
questions.explanation: Most CSF is absorbed through arachnoid villi projecting into dural venous sinuses, returning CSF to the bloodstream; a small amount is also absorbed perivascularly around penetrating brain vessels.
questions.modelAnswer:
By arachnoid villi and granulations into dural venous sinuses
A little amount is formed around cerebral vessels and from ependyma cells

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the branches of vertebral artery
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery gives off meningeal, posterior inferior cerebellar (PICA), posterior spinal, anterior spinal, and medullary (paramedian) branches as it ascends through the foramen magnum.
questions.modelAnswer: Meningeal, Posterior inferior cerebellar, posterior spinal, anterior spinal, medullary branches

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the beginning and termination of vertebral artery.
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery begins as a branch of the first (proximal) part of the subclavian artery and terminates at the lower border of the pons by joining the contralateral vertebral artery to form the basilar artery.
questions.modelAnswer:
Begins as a branch of first part of subclavian artery
Ends at lower border of pons by joining the other vertebral artery to form basilary artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the beginning and termination of basilar artery.
questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed at the lower border of the pons by the union of the two vertebral arteries and terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer:
It’s formed by union of right and left vertebral arteries at lower border of pons
Ends at upper border of pons by giving its two terminal branches “right and left posterior cerebral arteries”

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the branches of basilar artery
questions.explanation: The basilar artery gives off pontine (paramedian) branches, labyrinthine artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), superior cerebellar artery (SCA), and its terminal branches the posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Pontine branches, labyrinthine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, posterior cerebellar

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the arteries that form the circle of Willis
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis is formed anteriorly by the anterior cerebral arteries and anterior communicating artery, laterally by the internal carotid arteries and posterior communicating arteries, and posteriorly by the posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: ACA, anterior communicating artery, ICA, PCA, posterior communicating

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by anterior cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere (except occipital lobe), a one-inch strip of the superior lateral surface, and the medial part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial surface: All except occipital lobe
Lateral surface: One inch strip superiorly
Inferior surface: Medial part of orbital surface

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by middle cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral cerebral surface (excluding occipital pole and superior/inferior border strips), the lateral orbital surface, and the temporal pole.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lateral surface: large area except occipital lobe+ a strip along superior border+ a strip along inferior border
Inferior surface: lateral part of orbital surface+ temporal pole

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by posterior cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the medial and lateral occipital surfaces, the inferior temporal surface (except temporal pole), and contributes to the visual cortex via calcarine artery.
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial surface: occipital lobe
Lateral surface: occipital lobe+ strip along lower border of hemisphere
Inferior surface: tentorial part except temporal pole

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does the mesenchyme around Meckle’s cartilage give?
questions.explanation: Mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage (1st arch) differentiates into malleus, incus, sphenomandibular ligament, anterior ligament of malleus, and contributes to mandibular formation.
questions.modelAnswer: Mandible, Spehnomandibular ligament, Spine of sphenoid, Anterior ligament of malleus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What do chromaffin cells give?
questions.explanation: Chromaffin cells (neural crest derivatives) give rise to the adrenal medulla, paraganglia (including carotid and aortic bodies), and extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue throughout the body.
questions.modelAnswer: Adrenal medulla, carotid body, and paraganglia

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Compare between 2nd and 3rd arch. (according to aortic arch)
questions.explanation: The second pharyngeal arch arterial derivative largely regresses, leaving only the stapedial artery; the third arch forms the common carotid artery and the proximal internal carotid artery, with the external carotid arising as a sprout.
questions.modelAnswer:
2nd arch: disappear leaving stapedial artery
3rd arch: CCA, proximal part of ICA, and ECA arises as a sprout

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands (from its inferior wing) and the thymus (from its ventral wing), explaining the common origin of these structures.
questions.modelAnswer: Inferior parathyroid gland and epithelium of thymus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the 3 derivatives of intermaxillary segment.
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment (median nasal prominence) gives rise to the philtrum of the upper lip, the primary palate (premaxilla carrying the four incisor teeth), and the median part of the upper jaw.
questions.modelAnswer:
Philtrum of upper lip
Part of upper jaw that carries the 4 incisor teeth
1ry palate

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the 5 secondary brain vesicles and their derivatives in adult brain.
questions.explanation: The five secondary brain vesicles and their adult derivatives are: telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres), diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus), mesencephalon (midbrain), metencephalon (pons and cerebellum), and myelencephalon (medulla oblongata).
questions.modelAnswer:
Telencephalon: Cerebral hemisphere
Diencephalon: Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus
Mesencephalon: Midbrain
Metencephalon: Pons
Myelencephalon: Medulla

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mention the derivatives of neural crest.
questions.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate to form sensory ganglia (neuroblasts), autonomic ganglia, melanocytes, chromaffin cells, Schwann cells, meninges (pia and arachnoid), odontoblasts, and skeletal elements of branchial arches.
questions.keyConcept: Neural crest cell derivatives and migration
questions.modelAnswer: Neuroblast, Spongioblast, Melanocyte, Chromaffin cells, Odontoblasts and cartilaginous elements of the branchial arches

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention functions of the nervous system
questions.explanation: The nervous system maintains homeostasis, controls skeletal muscle activity, regulates glandular secretion, processes sensory information, and subserves higher mental functions including consciousness, learning, and memory.
questions.modelAnswer:
Maintains homeostasis
Control of muscles & glands
Control of mental function
Receive sensory impulses
Processing & integrating information

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Define synapse
questions.explanation: A synapse is a specialized functional junction between two neurons (or a neuron and an effector) where information is transmitted via neurotransmitter release, allowing communication between electrically separate cells.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the site of contact between 2 neurons with separate protoplasm (functional junction)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Enumerate functions of synapses
questions.explanation: Synaptic functions include unidirectional impulse transmission, convergence (multiple inputs to one neuron for intensity encoding), divergence (one neuron to multiple targets), and are primary sites of drug action.
questions.modelAnswer:
Transmission of impulses
Convergence of impulse: Collection of Impulses — intensity of impulses (intensification)
Divergence of impulses: spreading of impulses
The site of action of drugs

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare between chemical synapse & electric synapse regarding Def. & Characteristics
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses use neurotransmitter release and receptor activation for unidirectional, slower, drug-sensitive transmission; electrical synapses use gap junctions for bidirectional, faster signaling with no drug sensitivity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Chemical synapse
Def. Occur by release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic terminal (terminal button) traverse the synaptic cleft & affect postsynaptic membrane
Characteristics: Less common, Unidirectional, Less fast, Drug sensitive, Excitatory or inhibitory
Electric synapse
Def. Occur by passage of ions & small molecules through gap junction between 2 adjacent cells
Characteristics: More common, Bidirectional, Faster, No drug sensitivity, Excitatory only

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Illustrate the mechanism of chemical neurotransmission in synapses
questions.explanation: Chemical neurotransmission involves calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, ion channel modulation, postsynaptic potential changes, and subsequent neurotransmitter removal via reuptake, degradation, or diffusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic knob
NT crosses the cleft.
Combines with its specific receptor on postsynaptic membrane.
Changes the RMP of postsynaptic membrane by opening or closing channels.
Removal of NT.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: List the ways of removal of NT
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are removed from the synaptic cleft by presynaptic reuptake (active transport), enzymatic degradation at postsynaptic membrane, or passive diffusion away from the synapse.
questions.modelAnswer:
Active Reuptake by the presynaptic membrane
Inactivation by enzyme on postsynaptic membrane.
Passive diffusion away.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Define:
Neurohormone
Neuromodulator
Neurotransmitter
questions.explanation: A neurotransmitter is rapidly inactivated and acts briefly between neurons; a neuromodulator acts more slowly and long-term to alter synaptic effectiveness; a neurohormone is released into blood to act at distant targets.
questions.keyConcept: Distinction between neurotransmitter, neuromodulator, and neurohormone
questions.modelAnswer:
Neurohormone: A chemical substance secreted by a neuron into blood
Neuromodulator: A slowly inactivated (long acting) chemical substance secreted
Neurotransmitter: A chemical substance secreted by neurons to stimulate or inhibit other neurons

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the sites of release of Acetyl choline
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is released at CNS synapses (cortex, thalamus), all neuromuscular junctions, all autonomic preganglionic terminals, all postganglionic parasympathetic terminals, and some sympathetic terminals (sweat glands, skeletal muscle vessels).
questions.keyConcept: Acetylcholine release sites in nervous system
questions.modelAnswer:
Brain (cortex, thalamus)
NM junction
All preganglionic neurons
All postganglionic parasympathetic neurons
Some postganglionic sympathetic as sweat glands and blood vessels of skeletal muscles.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention effects of Norepinephrine
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is generally excitatory on alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction) and inhibitory on beta-2 receptors (bronchodilation, vasodilation), producing complex tissue-specific effects depending on receptor distribution.
questions.modelAnswer: Stimulatory on α1 receptors Inhibitory on β2 receptors

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the effect of GABA?
questions.explanation: GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through GABA-A receptors to increase chloride ion influx, causing membrane hyperpolarization and neuronal inhibition.
questions.modelAnswer: Inhibitory, by increasing the influx of Cl- causing hyperpolarization

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding adaptation, Touch receptors are rapidly adapting receptors while pain receptors are slowly adapting receptors
questions.explanation: Touch receptors (Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles) are rapidly adapting phasic receptors, while pain receptors (free nerve endings) are slowly adapting tonic receptors, reflecting their functional roles in sensory processing.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor adaptation rates and functional significance

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Enumerate properties of receptors
questions.explanation: Receptors have specificity for particular stimuli, demonstrate adequate stimulus, exhibit variable sensitivity, show adaptation (phasic vs tonic), generate graded potentials, and have low threshold for activation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Illustrate mechanism of receptors adaptation
questions.explanation: Receptor adaptation involves sodium channel inactivation during sustained stimulation, reducing generator potential amplitude; rapidly adapting receptors have quickly inactivating channels while slowly adapting ones maintain depolarization.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The resting membrane potential is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential (~-70mV) is closest to K+ equilibrium potential (~-90mV) because membrane permeability to K+ at rest exceeds that of other ions, allowing K+ leak channels to dominate.
questions.keyConcept: Resting membrane potential and K+ equilibrium

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Explain paradoxical cold sensation
questions.explanation: Paradoxical cold sensation occurs when skin temperature drops below 10C, activating cold receptors (normally activated at 10-40C) at the same time warm receptors are inhibited, creating the sensation of cold.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare between crude touch sensation & thermal sensation regarding ( Def. receptors & afferent neuron type)
questions.explanation: Crude touch uses free nerve endings and type A-delta fibers (discriminative touch uses Meissner's corpuscles with A-beta fibers); thermal sensation uses thermal receptors with A-delta (cold) and C fibers (warm).
questions.keyConcept: Touch and thermal sensation receptor differences

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the mechanism of stimulation of pain receptors.
questions.explanation: Pain receptors (nociceptors) are stimulated by intense mechanical/thermal/chemical stimuli that cause tissue damage, releasing bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, and prostaglandins that sensitize and activate nociceptors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare between reflex movements & voluntary movements regarding requirements
questions.explanation: Reflex movements require only the spinal cord (or brainstem) without conscious thought and have stereotyped patterns; voluntary movements require cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and conscious awareness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the clinical importance of stretch reflex
questions.explanation: The stretch reflex is clinically important for assessing muscle tone, detecting upper vs lower motor neuron lesions, and localizing spinal cord levels; it underlies the knee-jerk and other deep tendon reflexes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compare between nuclear bag fibers & nuclear chain fibers
questions.explanation: Nuclear bag fibers have central nuclei (multiple nuclei aggregated in fiber center), detect dynamic stretch, and innervated by large gamma motor neurons; nuclear chain fibers have elongated nuclei, detect static stretch, and innervated by smaller gamma neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is coma?
questions.explanation: Coma is a state of unarousable unconsciousness where the person cannot be awakened by sensory stimuli, caused by bilateral cerebral hemisphere dysfunction or damage to ascending reticular activating system.
questions.modelAnswer: Unconsciousness from which the person cannot be aroused

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is sleep?
questions.explanation: Sleep is a reversible physiological state of unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sufficient stimulation, distinct from coma which is unarousable.
questions.keyConcept: Sleep definition and distinction from coma
questions.modelAnswer: Physiological and spontaneous unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by stimuli

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the functions of sleep?
questions.explanation: Sleep functions include restoration of physiological processes, cognitive consolidation, memory encoding, thermoregulation, immune system maintenance, and neural plasticity required for development and learning.
questions.modelAnswer: Restoration of physiological & biochemical processes (Cognition, metabolic, thermal, caloric & immune processes) Helps learning & memory Neural plasticity (maturation)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the stages and EEG characteristics of very light sleep?
questions.explanation: Very light sleep (Stage N1) is characterized by theta wave EEG activity (4-8 Hz), vertex sharp waves, and loss of alpha rhythm, representing transition from wakefulness to sleep.
questions.modelAnswer: Theta waves

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What are the stages and EEG
questions.explanation: N2 sleep (light sleep) shows sleep spindles and K-complexes on EEG; N3 (deep sleep) shows delta waves; REM sleep shows theta rhythm with sawtooth waves and muscle atonia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the role of the piriform cortex in smell?
questions.explanation: The piriform cortex is the primary olfactory cortex responsible for perception and discrimination of odor quality, receiving direct input from the olfactory bulb via the lateral olfactory tract.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the role of the amygdala in smell?
questions.explanation: The amygdala processes emotional aspects of olfactory stimuli, particularly those associated with fear and reward, connecting olfactory information with emotional and behavioral responses.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the role of the enterorhinal cortex in smell?
questions.explanation: The enterorhinal cortex (area 28) is the major gateway for neocortical information to hippocampus, critical for forming and retrieving olfactory memories and spatial memory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is responsible for the conscious discrimination of odors?
questions.explanation: Conscious odor discrimination is mediated by the orbitofrontal and frontal neocortex, which receives processed olfactory information via thalamic relays, allowing identification and naming of odors.
options: Lateral & VM hypothalamus, septum, Amygdala, thalamus & basal ganglia

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the role of normal limbic system in maternal & sexual behavior?
questions.explanation: Normal limbic system function is essential for maternal behavior (nurturing and bonding) and proper sexual behavior, with the medial preoptic area and limbic circuits coordinating these instinctual behaviors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What factors can modify sexual behavior?
questions.explanation: Sexual behavior is modified by multiple factors including prefrontal cortex (executive control), social/cultural influences, psychological state, hormones, and olfactory cues acting through the limbic system.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the main function of the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus maintains internal homeostasis through autonomic control, regulates endocrine function via pituitary connection, controls food intake, temperature, thirst, and circadian rhythms.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which parts of the hypothalamus control autonomic responses?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus controls autonomic responses primarily through the posterior and lateral hypothalamus (sympathetic) and anterior/ventromedial regions (parasympathetic), via descending pathways to brainstem autonomic centers.
options: Regulation of food intake and appetite

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How does the hypothalamus control endocrine functions Through nervous control?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic neurons directly control the posterior pituitary via axonal projections, releasing oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH) into systemic circulation in response to neural stimuli.
options: Control of posterior pituitary gland leads to secret oxytocin & vasopressin
Control of Adrenal medulla leads to secret catecholamines

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: How does the hypothalamus control endocrine functions Through hormonal control?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones travel through the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system to control anterior pituitary hormone secretion, which then regulates peripheral endocrine glands.
options: Control of Anterior pituitary gland, which controls most body endocrine glands

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which part of the hypothalamus is the feeding center?
questions.explanation: The lateral hypothalamus contains the feeding (hunger) center; stimulation increases appetite and feeding behavior while destruction causes anorexia and weight loss.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which part of the hypothalamus is the satiety center?
questions.explanation: The ventromedial hypothalamus contains the satiety center; stimulation produces feeling of fullness and stops eating while destruction leads to hyperphagia and obesity.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Mention the cutaneous unencapsulated receptors?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous unencapsulated receptors include free nerve endings (pain, temperature), peritrichial endings around hair follicles (light touch), and Merkel's discs (fine touch); all lack a connective tissue capsule.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Mention the cutaneous encapsulated receptors?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous encapsulated receptors include Meissner's corpuscles (light touch), Pacinian corpuscles (vibration), Ruffini endings (stretch), and Merkel's discs are sometimes considered encapsulated; all have a surrounding connective tissue capsule.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What tumor is characterized by excessive production of catecholamines? And what is the treatment of it?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla; treatment includes alpha-methyl tyrosine (blocks tyrosine hydroxylase) and surgical removal, plus alpha/beta blockers for symptomatic control.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pheochromocytoma
α-methyl tyrosine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the rate limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, converting tyrosine to DOPA; it requires tetrahydropteridine and iron as cofactors and is subject to end-product inhibition.
questions.modelAnswer: Tyrosine hydroxylase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the fate of catecholamines?
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are cleared by active reuptake into presynaptic nerve terminals (uptake-1 mechanism) and enzymatic hydrolysis by enzymes like MAO and COMT, preventing prolonged receptor activation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Active uptake by sympathetic nerve endings
Enzymatic hydrolysis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What enzymes cause the oxidative deamination and inactivation of catecholamines?
questions.explanation: Monoamine oxidase (MAO), found in mitochondrial membranes of presynaptic terminals, causes oxidative deamination and inactivation of catecholamines, producing corresponding aldehydes.
questions.modelAnswer: Monoamine oxidase (MAO)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the primary end product of dopamine inactivation?
questions.explanation: Dopamine is primarily inactivated to homovanillic acid (HVA) via combined MAO and COMT activity; CSF HVA levels are used clinically to assess dopamine turnover.
questions.modelAnswer: Homovanillic acid (HVA)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the primary end product of epinephrine and norepinephrine enzymatic inactivation?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are metabolized primarily to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) via combined MAO and COMT pathways; 24-hour urinary VMA is diagnostic for pheochromocytoma.
questions.modelAnswer: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the neurodegenerative movement disorder characterized by insufficient dopamine production?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is the neurodegenerative movement disorder caused by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the striatum.
questions.modelAnswer: Parkinson Disease

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the immediate metabolic precursor of dopamine that can cross the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: L-DOPA (levodopa) is the immediate metabolic precursor of dopamine that crosses the blood-brain barrier via the large neutral amino acid transporter, where it is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase in the brain.
questions.keyConcept: L-DOPA as dopamine precursor crossing BBB
questions.modelAnswer: L-DOPA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the inhibitor of dopa-decarboxylase used in the treatment of Parkinson Disease?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa is a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor used in Parkinson's treatment; it prevents peripheral L-DOPA conversion to dopamine, increasing brain delivery and reducing peripheral side effects like nausea.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbidopa

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What enzyme is inhibited by a-methyl tyrosine in the treatment of pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation: Alpha-methyl tyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, blocking conversion of tyrosine to DOPA and reducing catecholamine production in pheochromocytoma.
questions.modelAnswer: Tyrosine hydroxylase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the neurotransmitter produced in the CNS, gastrointestinal tract & platelets?
questions.explanation: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is synthesized in CNS neurons (raphe nuclei), enterochromaffin cells of GI tract, and platelets, where it acts as a neurotransmitter, hormone, and local signaling molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: Serotonin (5-HT)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the end product of serotonin degradation?
questions.explanation: Serotonin is degraded to 5-hydroxyindolacetic acid (5-HIAA) via MAO; urinary 5-HIAA measurement is used to diagnose carcinoid tumors that overproduce serotonin.
questions.modelAnswer: 5-hydroxyindolacetic acid (5-HIAA)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What tumor is characterized by increased production of serotonin and decreased production of nicotinic acid?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors (argentaffinomas) produce excessive serotonin, causing flushing, diarrhea, and cardiac disease; they also decrease nicotinic acid (vitamin B3) synthesis because serotonin diverts tryptophan away from niacin production.
questions.modelAnswer: Carcinoid tumor (Argentaffinoma)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the hormone involved in regulating sleep patterns and follows a circadian rhythm? And how it is formed?
questions.explanation: Melatonin is the pineal hormone regulating circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles, synthesized from serotonin via N-acetylation and methylation in the pineal body under darkness-activated signaling.
questions.modelAnswer:
Melatonin
From serotonin in pineal body by acetylation and methylation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What happens in Vitamin B6 deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 (PLP) is the coenzyme for glutamate decarboxylase; deficiency reduces GABA synthesis, causing neuronal hyperexcitability, seizures, and hyperactivity.
questions.modelAnswer: Reduction in GABA levels with signs of hyperactivity and convulsions

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What factors can lead to melatonin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Melatonin deficiency can result from cigarettes (nicotine), caffeine, frequent stress, antidepressant drugs, and beta-blockers, all of which suppress pineal melatonin secretion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cigarettes
Caffeine
Frequent stress
Antidepressants
ß-blocker

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is histamine formed?
questions.explanation: Histamine is formed by pyridoxal phosphate (B6)-dependent decarboxylation of histidine, catalyzed by histidine decarboxylase, producing histamine and CO2.
questions.modelAnswer: Histamine is formed by decarboxylation of histidine in a reaction requiring PLP

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the role of histamine?
questions.explanation: Histamine mediates allergic inflammation, stimulates gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors, acts as a CNS neurotransmitter modulating arousal, and causes vasodilation via H1 receptors.
questions.modelAnswer:
Histamine mediates a wide range of cellular responses, including allergic and inflammatory reactions, gastric acid secretion
Act as a Neurotransmitter in CNS
Powerful vasodilator

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of histamine in the brain?
questions.explanation: In the brain, histamine functions as a neurotransmitter in the tuberomammillary nucleus projections, promoting wakefulness and arousal through H1 receptor activation.
questions.modelAnswer: Histamine acts as a Neurotransmitter in parts of the brain by mediating arousal.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the neurotransmitters that act as vasodilator?
questions.explanation: Histamine and nitric oxide are the primary neurotransmitter vasodilators; histamine acts via H1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle while NO acts directly on vascular smooth muscle to cause relaxation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Histamine
Nitric oxide

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is nitric oxide synthesized?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), producing L-citrulline and NO; this requires NADPH, oxygen, and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactors.
questions.modelAnswer: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine in a reaction catalyzed by nitric oxide synthase enzyme

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the functions of nitric oxide?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide causes vasodilation in cerebral/coronal arteries, relaxes GIT/urinary smooth muscle, stimulates hypothalamic hormone release, enables macrophage killing, and is used therapeutically (nitroglycerin for angina, inhaled NO for pulmonary hypertension).
questions.modelAnswer:
Vasodilatation in cerebral, coronary & muscle arteries
Relaxation of GIT & urinary tract
Stimulate release of hormones from hypothalamus
Produced from macrophage, monocytes & neutrophils to kill microorganisms
Pharmacological functions: Nitroglycerin - treat angina; Inhalation of NO - treat pulmonary hypertension & pulmonary edema without decrease systemic blood pressure

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is derived from tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine is the amino acid precursor for catecholamine neurotransmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine), which are synthesized via tyrosine hydroxylase, DOPA decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, and PNMT.
questions.modelAnswer: Catecholamines (Dopamine, Norepinephrine, Epinephrine)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Where are dopamine and norepinephrine synthesized?
questions.explanation: Dopamine and norepinephrine are synthesized in the brain (as CNS neurotransmitters) and in adrenal medulla chromaffin cells (mainly norepinephrine which is then methylated to epinephrine).
questions.modelAnswer: In the brain and function as neurotransmitters

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Epinephrine is synthesized in_________ and the primary end product in the adrenal medulla of newborns is _________
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized in the adrenal medulla from norepinephrine via phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT); in newborns, the primary catecholamine end product is norepinephrine due to immature PNMT activity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What happens to epinephrine with advancing age?
questions.explanation: With advancing age, epinephrine production dramatically increases, largely dependent upon cortisol levels since cortisol induces PNMT expression in the adrenal medulla.
questions.modelAnswer: Dramatically raised, depending upon cortisol levels

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is histamine synthesized from? And What is the enzyme required for histamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Histamine is synthesized from histidine by histidine decarboxylase, a PLP-dependent enzyme, producing histamine and CO2; this reaction is irreversible.
questions.modelAnswer:
Histidine
Histidine decarboxylase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The coenzyme required for histamine synthesis is_________ and cells secrete it is_________
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, active form of B6) is the required coenzyme for histamine synthesis via histidine decarboxylase; histamine is secreted by mast cells, basophils, and enterochromaffin cells.
questions.keyConcept: PLP coenzyme and mast cell histamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the major functions of histamine? (Name two)
questions.explanation: Major histamine functions include mediating Type I hypersensitivity (allergic reactions), stimulating gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors, and acting as a CNS neurotransmitter promoting arousal.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mediating allergic and inflammatory reactions.
gastric acid secretion.
as a neurotransmitter in parts of the brain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Is histamine a vasodilator? If true, what else? And if false, why?
questions.explanation: True, histamine is a vasodilator; another vasodilator neurotransmitter is nitric oxide, which acts via cGMP pathway on vascular smooth muscle.
questions.modelAnswer:
True
Nitric oxide

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is nitric oxide synthesized? And What enzyme catalyzes the synthesis of nitric oxide?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) enzyme, producing NO and L-citrulline in a five-electron oxidation reaction requiring multiple cofactors.
questions.modelAnswer:
From L-arginine
Nitric oxide synthase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is glycine synthesized from? And what is the enzyme catalyzes its formation?
questions.explanation: Glycine is synthesized from serine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT), which transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate, forming glycine and N5,N10-methylene THF.
questions.modelAnswer:
Serine
Serine hydroxy-methyltransferase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is glycine removed from the synapse?
questions.explanation: Glycine is removed from the synaptic cleft by high-affinity sodium-dependent transporters (GlyT1 and GlyT2), allowing rapid termination of inhibitory signaling and recycling for neurotransmitter reuse.
questions.modelAnswer: Reuptake through high-affinity transporter

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the biogenic amines neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Biogenic amine neurotransmitters include acetylcholine (not technically a biogenic amine but often grouped) and the monoamines: catecholamines (dopamine, NE, E), serotonin (5-HT), and histamine.
questions.modelAnswer:
Acetylcholine
Monoamines

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the effects of acetylcholine?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine has mostly excitatory effects at neuromuscular junctions (causing muscle contraction) and in autonomic ganglia, though it can be inhibitory in some cardiovascular reflexes via vagal stimulation.
questions.modelAnswer: Mostly excitatory effects

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is Myasthenia gravis?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder with antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable muscle weakness that worsens with activity.
questions.modelAnswer: A chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disease causing weakness in the skeletal muscles

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the primary end product of catecholamine synthesis in the adrenal medulla?
questions.explanation: In the adrenal medulla, norepinephrine is the primary catecholamine end product; most norepinephrine is subsequently methylated to epinephrine by PNMT, but norepinephrine remains a major secreted product.
questions.modelAnswer: Norepinephrine (NE)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What happens when there are elevated levels of excitatory amino acids?
questions.explanation: Elevated excitatory amino acids (especially glutamate) cause excitotoxicity via excessive calcium influx, activating destructive enzymes, generating free radicals, and leading to neuronal death; implicated in stroke and neurodegenerative diseases.
questions.modelAnswer: Neurotoxicity resulting in neuronal death or injury

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through GABA-A (ionotropic, Cl- channel) and GABA-B (metabotropic, G-protein coupled) receptors.
questions.modelAnswer: GABA (Gamma Aminobutyric Acid)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is GABA derived from?
questions.explanation: GABA is derived from glutamic acid (glutamate) via decarboxylation catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), a PLP-dependent enzyme; this is an irreversible reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamic acid

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the classification of neurotransmitters based on functions?
questions.explanation: Based on function, neurotransmitters are classified as excitatory (causing depolarization/action potentials), inhibitory (causing hyperpolarization), or modulatory (altering neuronal sensitivity without direct excitation/inhibition).
questions.modelAnswer:
Excitatory
Inhibitory

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are examples of excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters include glutamate (principal excitatory NT in CNS) and aspartate, both acting through ionotropic (NMDA, AMPA, kainate) and metabotropic receptors.
questions.modelAnswer:
Glutamate
Aspartate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through NMDA, AMPA, kainate, and mGluR receptors; excessive activity causes excitotoxicity.
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Where are neurotransmitters stored?
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles (secretory vesicles) at presynaptic terminals, either small clear vesicles (acetylcholine, amino acids) or large dense-core vesicles (catecholamines, peptides).
questions.modelAnswer: In secretory vesicles (synaptic vesicles) before release into the synaptic cleft

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the substrates for glutamate transaminase?
questions.explanation: Glutamate transaminase (GOT/AST) uses alpha-ketoglutarate and L-aspartate as substrates to produce glutamate and oxaloacetate in a reversible PLP-dependent transamination reaction.
questions.modelAnswer:
α- ketoglutarate
L-aspartate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is ammonia utilized in the conversion of glutamate to glutamine?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is incorporated into glutamate by glutamine synthetase to form glutamine, consuming ATP; this is the primary mechanism for removing ammonia in the brain and preventing neurotoxicity.
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonia is used by glutamine synthetase to convert glutamate to glutamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acids can produce both glucose and ketone bodies?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, threonine, and isoleucine are glucogenic-amino acids that can be converted to pyruvate or TCA intermediates (producing glucose via gluconeogenesis) and also generate ketone body precursors.
questions.modelAnswer:
Tyrosine
phenylalanine
tryptophan
threonine
isoleucine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the main pathway of deamination for amino acids?
questions.explanation: Transamination (via aminotransferases using PLP) is the major pathway for amino acid deamination, transferring the amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, which then undergoes oxidative deamination by GDH.
questions.modelAnswer: L-glutamate dehydrogenase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme is responsible for the oxidative deamination of D-AAs and glycine?
questions.explanation: D-amino acid oxidase (D-AA oxidase flavoprotein) is the FAD-dependent enzyme responsible for oxidative deamination of D-amino acids and glycine, converting them to corresponding alpha-keto acids and ammonia.
questions.modelAnswer: D-AA oxidase flavoprotein

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of D-AA oxidase flavoprotein?
questions.explanation: D-AA oxidase flavoprotein converts D-amino acids to alpha-keto acids by removing the amino group, eliminating the asymmetry of the alpha-carbon atom and producing a racemic mixture with L-forms.
questions.modelAnswer: Conversion of D-amino acids to the α-keto acid will remove the asymmetry of the α-carbon atom.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the product of the transdeamination of glutamine?
questions.explanation: Transdeamination of glutamine involves glutamine transaminase (producing glutamate and alpha-keto glutaramate) followed by omega-amidase, ultimately yielding alpha-ketoglutarate as the carbon skeleton product.
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the role of glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing ammonia and NAD(P)H; this is the key reaction linking amino acid metabolism with TCA cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Conversion of glutamate to α-ketoglutarate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the major pathway of oxidative deamination?
questions.explanation: L-glutamate dehydrogenase is the major pathway for oxidative deamination of amino acids in mammals, converting L-glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate with production of ammonia and NAD(P)H.
questions.keyConcept: L-GDH as main oxidative deamination enzyme
questions.modelAnswer: L-glutamate dehydrogenase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which organs mainly carry out oxidative deamination?
questions.explanation: Liver and kidney are the primary organs for oxidative deamination, but heart, brain, and skeletal muscle also carry out this reaction, contributing to amino acid nitrogen disposal.
questions.modelAnswer:
Liver, kidney
heart, brain, and muscle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What coenzyme is required for L-glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: L-glutamate dehydrogenase requires NAD+ (for oxidative deamination) or NADP+ (for reductive amination) as coenzymes, reflecting its reversible nature in nitrogen metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer:
NAD
NADP

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: NAD+ is used in oxidative deamination and NADP+ in reductive amination.
questions.explanation: True: NAD+ is the coenzyme for oxidative deamination ( glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate), while NADP+ is used in reductive amination (alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate), maintaining redox balance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What stimulates L-glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: ADP and GDP (guanosine diphosphate) allosterically stimulate L-glutamate dehydrogenase, increasing ammonia production during energy deficit states when more amino acids need to be catabolized.
questions.modelAnswer:
ADP
GDP

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What inhibits L-glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: ATP, GTP, and NADH allosterically inhibit L-glutamate dehydrogenase, preventing excessive ammonia production when energy status is adequate and reducing glutamate catabolism.
questions.modelAnswer:
ATP
GTP
NADH

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the coenzyme of the enzyme D-AA oxidase?
questions.explanation: D-amino acid oxidase is a flavoprotein requiring FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) as its prosthetic group, which accepts electrons during the oxidative deamination reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: FAD

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In which organs is D-AA oxidase found?
questions.explanation: D-amino acid oxidase is found primarily in liver and kidney peroxisomes, where it metabolizes D-amino acids from dietary sources and bacterial cell walls.
questions.modelAnswer: Liver and kidney

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the enzyme responsible for nonoxidative deamination of glutamine?
questions.explanation: Deamidases (glutaminase for glutamine, asparaginase for asparagine) are the enzymes responsible for nonoxidative deamination, releasing ammonia directly by hydrolyzing the amide group.
questions.modelAnswer: Deamidases

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What substrates does Ketoglutarate-D-AA oxidase flavoprotein act on?
questions.explanation: Ketoglutarate-D-AA oxidase flavoprotein acts on D-amino acids and glycine as substrates, performing transdeamination reactions that link amino acid metabolism to TCA cycle intermediates.
questions.modelAnswer:
D-AAs
glycine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What happens to glutamine in the liver?
questions.explanation: In the liver, glutamine is cleaved by glutaminase to produce glutamate and ammonia; the ammonia enters the urea cycle while glutamate enters energy metabolism or gluconeogenesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Cleaved by glutaminase enzyme to produce ammonia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What amino acids can’t go through transamination?
questions.explanation: Lysine, threonine, proline, and hydroxyproline cannot undergo transamination because they lack an alpha-amino group or have secondary amino groups that are not recognized by aminotransferases.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lysine
Threonine
Proline
Hydroxyproline

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What enzyme converts pyruvate to alanine in muscles?
questions.explanation: Alanine transaminase (ALT) catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to alanine in muscles, using glutamate as the amino donor; this is part of the glucose-alanine cycle transporting nitrogen to liver.
questions.modelAnswer: ALT enzyme

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of L-AA oxidase?
questions.explanation: L-amino acid oxidase catalyzes the oxidative deamination of L-amino acids to corresponding alpha-keto acids, producing hydrogen peroxide and ammonia; FMN is its required cofactor.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidative deamination of L-amino acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the process of non-oxidative deamination for glutamine and asparagine?
questions.explanation: Non-oxidative deamination of glutamine and asparagine is catalyzed by specific deamidases (glutaminase, asparaginase), releasing NH3 which enters the urea cycle in liver or is excreted in urine by kidneys.
questions.modelAnswer: Deamidases release NH3 which enters urea cycle in the liver, or passes in urine in the kidney.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Where does NH3 released by deamidases in the liver go?
questions.explanation: NH3 released by hepatic deamidases enters the urea cycle in hepatocytes, where it is combined with CO2 and ammonia from other sources to form urea for renal excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Urea cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Where does NH3 released by deamidases in the kidney go?
questions.explanation: NH3 released by renal deamidases is not converted to urea but diffuses into the tubular lumen and is excreted directly in urine as ammonium ion.
questions.modelAnswer: Urine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the sources of ammonia NH3?
questions.explanation: Sources of ammonia include amino acid catabolism (transamination, oxidative deamination), purine/pyrimidine catabolism, glutaminase action, amine oxidation, and intestinal bacterial metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer:
Catabolism of amino acids
catabolism of purine and pyrimidine
glutaminase enzyme
Catabolism of amines
intestinal bacteria

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the synthetic fates of ammonia?
questions.explanation: Synthetic fates of ammonia include incorporation into non-essential amino acids via reductive amination (glutamate from alpha-ketoglutarate) and glutamine synthesis via glutamine synthetase.
questions.modelAnswer:
Synthesis of non essential amino acids
Synthesis of glutamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver?
questions.explanation: The major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver is urea synthesis via the urea cycle, which converts two molecules of ammonia (one free, one from aspartate) into one urea molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: Synthesis of urea

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is hepatic encephalopathy diagnosed?
questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is diagnosed by excluding other causes of altered mental status, identifying precipitating factors (infection, bleeding, electrolytes), and observing rapid improvement with ammonia-lowering treatment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Exclusion of other causes of encephalopathy
identification of the precipitating cause
rapid response to empiric treatment

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does lactulose help in the reduction of ammonia production?
questions.explanation: Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying colonic contents (conversion to lactic/acetic acid), reducing ammonia absorption, and decreasing ammonia-producing bacteria through osmotic catharsis.
questions.modelAnswer: Inhibits intestinal ammonia production by reducing colonic bacterial load and acidifying the gut lumen

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of neomycin in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Neomycin treats hepatic encephalopathy by killing intestinal bacteria that produce ammonia from protein catabolism, reducing the ammonia load reaching the liver through portal circulation.
questions.modelAnswer: Kills intestinal bacteria

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Name three substances used to increase ammonia clearance.
questions.explanation: Sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, and sodium phenylacetate are ammonia scavengers used to increase nitrogen excretion in urea cycle disorders and hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sodium benzoate
sodium phenylbutyrate
sodium phenylacetate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How does sodium benzoate contribute to ammonia clearance?
questions.explanation: Sodium benzoate conjugates with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is rapidly excreted in urine, effectively removing one nitrogen atom from the body per molecule of benzoate.
questions.modelAnswer: Interacts with glycine to form Hippurate, which is then excreted in the urine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the role of L-ornithine-L-aspartate in hepatic encephalopathy treatment?
questions.explanation: L-ornithine-L-aspartate (LOLA) stimulates the urea cycle by providing substrates (ornithine and aspartate) for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, enhancing ammonia fixation and disposal.
questions.modelAnswer: Stimulates the urea cycle, leading to the loss of ammonia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the effect of hyperammonia on brain function?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonia decreases Krebs cycle activity and ATP production, reduces GABA synthesis (causing hyperexcitability), disrupts cerebral electrical activity, causes cerebral edema, and increases serotonin production.
questions.modelAnswer:
Decrease in Krebs’ cycle and ATP production
decrease in GABA (neurotransmitter)
interference with electric activity in the brain
cerebral edema, and increased serotonin production

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the causes of hyperammonemia?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia causes include acquired forms (liver cirrhosis, hepatitis, portosystemic shunts) and congenital forms (urea cycle enzyme deficiencies, ornithine transporter defects, N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency).
questions.modelAnswer:
Acquired hyperammonemia due to liver diseases
congenital hyperammonemia due to deficiencies in urea cycle enzymes, membrane-associated ornithine transporter, or N-acetyl glutamate synthase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the first step of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The first step of the urea cycle is carbamoyl phosphate synthesis from ammonia and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondrial matrix, consuming 2 ATP.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the enzyme responsible for carbamoyl phosphate synthesis?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is the enzyme responsible for carbamoyl phosphate synthesis in the first step of the urea cycle, requiring N-acetylglutamate as an obligate activator.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the enzyme catalyzing the second step of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the second step of the urea cycle, transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, forming citrulline.
questions.modelAnswer: Ornithine transcarbamoylase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the second step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The second step of the urea cycle is citrulline synthesis, catalyzed by ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC), occurring in the mitochondrial matrix.
questions.modelAnswer: Citrulline synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the third step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The third step of the urea cycle is argininosuccinate synthesis, catalyzed by argininosuccinate synthetase, where citrulline combines with aspartate in the cytosol.
questions.modelAnswer:
Argininosuccinate synthesis
Argininosuccinate synthetase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the fourth step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The fourth step of the urea cycle is cleavage of argininosuccinate by argininosuccinate lyase to form arginine and fumarate in the cytosol.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cleavage of argininosuccinate
Argininosuccinate lyase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the final step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The final step of the urea cycle is cleavage of arginine by arginase to form urea and ornithine, with ornithine being transported back to mitochondria to repeat the cycle.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cleavage of arginine
Arginase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate and subject to substrate availability control.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Synthesis of urea occurs in the liver and excretion by the kidney
questions.explanation: Urea synthesis occurs exclusively in the liver mitochondria and cytosol, while excretion is performed by the kidneys; the liver synthesizes urea from ammonia and the kidneys filter and excrete it in urine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme is present in the cytosol and used in pyrimidine synthesis? And what is its other mitochondrial enzyme used in urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrial enzyme used in pyrimidine synthesis is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II), distinct from the cytosolic enzyme; the question may refer to amidophosphoribosyltransferase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
questions.modelAnswer:
CPS II
CPS I

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How many ATP molecules and high energy bonds are utilized in the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle consumes 3 ATP molecules (equivalent to 4 high-energy phosphate bonds): 2 ATP for CPS I reaction and 1 ATP for argininosuccinate synthetase (AMP + PPi effectively = 2 ATP).
questions.modelAnswer:
3 ATP
4 High energy bonds

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the main fate of urea?
questions.explanation: The main fate of urea is renal excretion in urine; approximately 20-25g of urea is filtered and excreted daily in adults, with small amounts lost in sweat.
questions.modelAnswer: Excreted in urine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What activates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I)?
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (NAG), synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase, is the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.
questions.modelAnswer: N-acetylglutamate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the relationship between the urea cycle and the citric acid cycle?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle and citric acid cycle are linked through fumarate (from argininosuccinate cleavage) which enters the TCA cycle, and aspartate (from TCA cycle transamination) which provides nitrogen for urea synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin), preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
options: A condition caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin reductase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin biosynthesis
A condition caused by a deficiency of homocystinuria

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the clinical pictures of phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation: PKU clinical features include intellectual disability (if untreated), hypopigmentation (decreased tyrosine reduces melanin), and characteristic mousy/musty odor from phenylacetate accumulation in urine and sweat.
options: Urine with a bad mousy odor

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How is phenylketonuria treated?
questions.explanation: PKU treatment involves lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction with tyrosine supplementation (since tyrosine becomes essential); with defective BH4 metabolism, DOPA and 5-HTP supplementation is also required.
options: A diet low in phenylalanine, supplementation of tyrosine
Giving DOPA and serotonin if there is dihydrobiopterin deficiency

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine and their ketoacids.
options: A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in branched-chain amino acid catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in phenylalanine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tyrosine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tryptophan catabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the effects of maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: MSUD manifests as mental retardation, developmental delay, feeding difficulties, and characteristic sweet maple syrup/burnt sugar odor of urine from accumulating branched-chain ketoacids; untreated cases often fatal in infancy.
options: Mental retardation and may lead to early death
The urine has a sweet smell-like maple syrup or burned sugar

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the treatment for maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: MSUD treatment requires lifelong restriction of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) in diet, with careful monitoring of amino acid levels to prevent neurological damage.
options: A diet low in branched-chain amino acids

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following are involved in the mechanism of action of morphine Except
questions.explanation: Morphine's effects are primarily mediated by mu (not kappa) opioid receptors; it also inhibits calcium influx (reducing transmitter release), increases K+ efflux (causing hyperpolarization), and reduces emotional pain response.
questions.keyConcept: Mu vs kappa opioid receptor activation
options: Most effects are mediated by activation of kappa receptors
Inhibition of calcium influx resulting in inhibition of transmitter release
Increase in K outflux resulting in hyperpolarization of neuronal membrane
Reduction of emotional response to pain

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Indications of morphine do not include
questions.explanation: Morphine is indicated for cancer pain, pulmonary edema (reduces preload and anxiety), and anesthesia adjunct; it is contraindicated in head injury (can worsen ICP and mask pupillary signs).
options: Acute pulmonary edema in acute left ventricular failure & myocardial infarction

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Most serious adverse effect/s of morphine
questions.explanation: The most serious adverse effects of morphine are respiratory depression (potentially fatal) and psychological/physical dependence with tolerance development upon chronic use.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Constipation associated with the use of morphine may be relieved by
questions.explanation: Morphine-induced constipation is relieved by stool softeners (docusate), stimulant laxatives, and peripherally-acting opioid antagonists (methylnaltrexone) that don't reverse analgesia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not common between pethidine & tramadol
questions.explanation: Pethidine and tramadol both have analgesic properties and can cause seizures at high doses, but tramadol's action is only partially reversed by naloxone (has non-opioid mechanisms), unlike pethidine.
options: Increase risk of convulsions with high doses

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Neuropathic pain may be managed by
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain management includes tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, gabapentin), and atypical opioids (tramadol), all acting on different pain pathways.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves supplying the scalp is derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) is the only scalp nerve derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves; all other listed nerves are derived from ventral rami (cervical plexus).
questions.keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve dorsal ramus origin

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The posterior triangle of the neck
questions.explanation: The posterior triangle is bounded by sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, and clavicle (not mandible); it is roofed by the superficial fascia and prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
options: Is bordered by sternocleidomastoid, mandible and trapezius
Has the accessory nerve beneath fascia of its floor
Is roofed by prevertebral layer of fascia
Contains trunks of the brachial plexus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The anterior triangle of the neck, include the following
questions.explanation: The anterior triangle has four subdivisions (muscular, carotid, digastric, submental); the occipital triangle is part of the posterior triangle, not anterior triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding tentorium cerebelli
questions.explanation: The tentorium cerebelli roofs over the posterior cranial fossa (not middle); its free border is attached to the anterior clinoid process (not post clinoid), and oculomotor/trochlear nerves pierce dura at this junction.
options: It roofs over middle cranial fossa
Its free border is attached to anterior clinoid process
Its attached border is attached to post clinoid process
It includes transverse venous sinus in its attached border
Oculomotor and trochlear nerves pierce dura at the point of crossing of its free & attached borders

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The falx cerebri
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres and contains the superior sagittal sinus in its superior border; the diaphragma sellae separates the pituitary from the brain.
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the
questions.explanation: Denticulate ligaments are pial extensions that anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater laterally; the coccygeal ligament (filum terminale externum) attaches the cord terminus to the coccyx.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The ventral grey column of the spinal cord contains the following groups of nerve cells Except
questions.explanation: The ventral grey column contains dorsomedial, ventrolateral, intermediolateral, and central groups; the retrodorsolateral group is found in the dorsal horn (lamina IX), not ventral horn.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (mesencephalon), not hindbrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Brain stem includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the cerebellum and cerebral aqueduct are not part of the brain stem proper (cerebral aqueduct connects third and fourth ventricles).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cranial part of the accessory nerve arises from
questions.explanation: The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla, carrying fibers that eventually join the vagus nerve to innervate laryngeal muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The right spinal lemniscus carries sensations of
questions.explanation: The right spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature sensation from the left side of the body (crossed fibers from spinothalamic tract); proprioception is carried in the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
options: Pain and temperature from left side of the body
Conscious proprioception from left side of the body
Muscle tone from right side of body

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The gracile and cuneate tracts of the spinal cord are supplied by
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate tracts are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries (branches of vertebral artery) and radicular arteries; the anterior spinal artery supplies anterior cord structures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced
questions.explanation: In adults, lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace (below L2 where spinal cord terminates); the needle passes through skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura, and arachnoid.
options: Below or above tip of 4th lumbar spine

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete section of spinal cord above C5 results in
questions.explanation: Complete transection of the spinal cord above C5 results in quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs) due to interruption of all descending motor pathways at the cervical level, along with respiratory compromise.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hemisection of spinal cord gives the following symptoms on the same side below the level of lesion
questions.explanation: In spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard), ipsilateral loss below lesion includes proprioception (dorsal columns) and upper motor neuron signs (corticospinal tract); pain/temperature loss is contralateral (spinothalamic decussation).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The following occur in Brown Sequard Syndrome Except
questions.explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, the LMN lesion at the level of lesion is ipsilateral (not contralateral); the lesion involves corticospinal tract (ipsi UMN signs) and dorsal columns (ipsi proprioception).
options: Ipsilateral UMN lesion below level of lesion
Contralateral loss of exteroceptive sensations below level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of proprioceptive sensations below level of lesion
