Contralateral L.M.N. lesion at same level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature at same level of lesion

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Upper motor neuron lesion is characterized by
questions.explanation: UMN lesion is characterized by spasticity (hypertonia), hyperreflexia, Babinski sign (plantar extension), and retained muscle bulk initially; option E (plantar flexion) describes normal reflex.
options: Plantar flexion of big toe on scratching skin of sole

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lower motor neuron lesion is characterized by
questions.explanation: LMN lesion is characterized by flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, muscle wasting, fasciculations, decreased/absent reflexes, and no Babinski sign (plantar reflex absent or normal flexion).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Syringomyelia first affects
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia (fluid-filled cavity in central spinal cord) first affects crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution.
options: Pain and temperature on both sides of the body
Pain and temperature on one side of the body

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hind brain (Rhombencephalon) includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (mesencephalon), containing cerebral peduncles with corticospinal tracts.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Brain stem includes the following Except
questions.explanation: The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the cerebellum is a distinct hindbrain derivative that overlies the fourth ventricle but is not part of the brain stem proper.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cranial part of the accessory nerve arises from
questions.explanation: The cranial part of accessory nerve arises from nucleus ambiguus in the medulla (fibers that join vagus for laryngeal innervation); the spinal part arises from C1-C5 spinal cord levels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The right spinal lemniscus carries sensations of
questions.explanation: The right spinal lemniscus carries crossed pain and temperature sensation from the left body (fibers have decussated at spinal cord levels before ascending in the spinothalamic tract).
options: Pain and temperature from left side of the body
Conscious proprioception from left side of the body
Muscle tone from right side of body

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The gracile and cuneate tracts of the spinal cord are supplied by
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate tracts are supplied by posterior spinal arteries and radicular arteries; the anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord including corticospinal tracts.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace (corresponding to below or above the L4 spinous process tip), which is well below the conus medullaris (L1-L2 in adults).
options: Below or above tip of 4th lumbar spine

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Complete section of spinal cord above C5 results in
questions.explanation: Complete cervical cord transection above C5 causes quadriplegia with loss of all motor function below the lesion, including respiratory muscles if the lesion is high enough to affect C3-C5 phrenic nerve origins.

questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.subject: Anatomy

options: Ipsilateral UMN lesion below level of lesion
Contralateral loss of exteroceptive sensations below level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of proprioceptive sensations below level of lesion

Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature at same level of lesion

questions.explanation: UMN lesion features: spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive; does NOT include hypotonia, marked wasting, or restricted paralysis (those are LMN features).

questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery supply:
questions.explanation: ACA supplies the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory for lower limb), medial aspect of frontal/parietal lobes; auditory cortex is supplied by MCA, not ACA.

questions.text: Arterial supply of upper 1/2 of internal capsule is derived from:

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute requirement for the brain at all times?
questions.explanation: The brain absolutely requires glucose and oxygen at all times; it cannot use fatty acids as an energy source and depends almost exclusively on glucose oxidation for ATP production.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In fasting conditions, glucose is provided for the brain by
questions.explanation: In fasting, brain glucose comes from hepatic glycogenolysis (immediately) and gluconeogenesis from lactate, amino acids, and glycerol (sustained); intestine is not a source during fasting.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Brain cells uptake glucose by
questions.explanation: Brain cells uptake glucose via GLUT1 (blood-brain barrier) and GLUT3 (neurons); GLUT2 is in liver/pancreas, GLUT4 is insulin-dependent in muscle/adipose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glucose uptake by the brain is
questions.explanation: Brain glucose uptake is insulin-independent; GLUT1 and GLUT3 are constitutively active at the blood-brain barrier and neuronal membranes, ensuring constant glucose supply.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Brain cells oxidize glucose to
questions.explanation: Brain cells completely oxidize glucose to CO2 and H2O via aerobic metabolism in mitochondria, producing 30-32 ATP per glucose molecule; they do not produce lactate or ketone bodies under normal conditions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In brain cells, glucose is phosphorylated by
questions.explanation: Brain uses hexokinase (not glucokinase) to phosphorylate glucose, giving it high affinity for glucose and allowing uptake even at low blood glucose concentrations.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glucose 6-phosphate is utilized in which pathway in brain cells?
questions.explanation: Glucose 6-phosphate in brain cells enters glycolysis; the pentose phosphate pathway also operates for nucleotide synthesis, but glycolysis is the main utilization pathway.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the importance of HMP pathway in the brain cells?
questions.explanation: HMP pathway's main importance in brain is generating NADPH for antioxidant defense (via glutathione reductase) and nucleotide synthesis; NADPH protects against oxidative stress which is critical for neurons.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hormones and neurotransmitters
questions.explanation: Hormones and neurotransmitters are signal molecules for cell-cell communication, derived from amino acids (nitrogenous) but also include non-nitrogenous compounds like steroid hormones.
options: are signal molecules used for cell-cell communication.
are mostly polypeptides or nitrogenous compounds, both derived from amino-acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following aminoacids may act as a neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glycine, glutamic acid (glutamate), and GABA are all amino acid neurotransmitters; glycine and GABA are inhibitory, glutamate is excitatory.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA) is produced by
questions.explanation: GABA is produced by decarboxylation of glutamic acid via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), requiring PLP (vitamin B6) as cofactor; both a and c are correct.
options: a reaction that requires vitamin B6 derived cofactor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the aminoacid neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate is excitatory, glycine/GABA are inhibitory; glycine is in collagen; glutamate produces MSG; all above is correct.
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen aminoacids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other aminoacids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Catecholamines
questions.explanation: Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) function as both hormones (adrenal medulla) and neurotransmitters (CNS/autonomic nervous system); both a and b are true.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Catecholamines
questions.explanation: Catecholamines contain the catechol (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) ring and are synthesized from tyrosine (not glycine); tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme.
options: contain the catechol (3,4-dihydroxy-phenyl) ring in their structure.
are synthesized from the aminoacid glycine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: L-Dopa (Dihydroxyphenylalanine) is
questions.explanation: L-DOPA is produced from tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase (not from dopamine); dopamine is synthesized from L-DOPA by DOPA decarboxylase. Option D (neither) is correct.
options: converted to tyrosine by a hydroxylase enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis is
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step by hydroxylating tyrosine to form DOPA; both formation of DOPA and hydroxylation of tyrosine describe the same step.
